history.heading: The Magyar conquest
paragraphs: The Carpathian Basin was home to Celts, Romans (the province of Pannonia), Huns and Avars before the Magyars, a people from the Ural region, arrived in 895 under Prince Árpád. In 1000 Stephen I was crowned the first King of Hungary and converted the country to Christianity; he is the national patron saint.

The medieval Kingdom of Hungary was a major European power. The Mongol invasion of 1241–42 devastated it, but it recovered, and under King Matthias Corvinus in the 15th century it was a centre of Renaissance culture.

history.heading: Ottomans and Habsburgs
paragraphs: The Ottoman victory at the Battle of Mohács in 1526 split Hungary into three parts for 150 years: Ottoman, Habsburg and the principality of Transylvania. After the Ottomans were expelled in the late 17th century, Hungary came under Habsburg rule.

The 1848 revolution, led by Lajos Kossuth, was crushed with Russian help. The Compromise of 1867 created Austria-Hungary, a dual monarchy in which Hungary had wide self-rule, and Budapest grew into a great city.

history.heading: Trianon, war and communism
paragraphs: After defeat in the First World War, the Treaty of Trianon (1920) cost Hungary about two-thirds of its territory, leaving millions of Hungarians in neighbouring countries, a lasting national trauma. Hungary allied with Nazi Germany in the Second World War; in 1944, about 440,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in a few months.

A Soviet-backed communist regime took power. The 1956 Hungarian Revolution was crushed by Soviet tanks. Under János Kádár, Hungary developed "goulash communism", a relatively liberal form of socialism.

history.heading: Democracy and the EU
paragraphs: In 1989 Hungary opened its border with Austria, helping bring down the Iron Curtain, and peacefully transitioned to democracy. It joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004. Viktor Orbán's Fidesz party won power in 2010 and dominated politics in the years that followed.

culture.heading: Language and the arts
paragraphs: Hungarian (Magyar) is a Uralic language, unrelated to its neighbours' Indo-European languages. Most Hungarians are Christian, mainly Catholic, with Calvinist and Lutheran minorities.

Hungary has produced composers Franz Liszt, Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály, and many scientists and inventors, including those behind the Rubik's Cube. Budapest, with the Danube banks, Buda Castle and Parliament, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and famous for its thermal baths.

culture.heading: Food and sport
paragraphs: Hungarian cuisine is famous for paprika, goulash (gulyás), pörkölt, lángos and chimney cake, and wines such as Tokaji and Egri Bikavér. Pálinka is a fruit brandy.

Hungary has won a remarkable number of Olympic medals relative to its size, especially in water polo, fencing, swimming and kayaking. The football team of the 1950s, the "Golden Team" with Ferenc Puskás, is legendary.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Hungary is a parliamentary republic with a unicameral National Assembly, a prime minister leading the government and a president elected by parliament. Fidesz has held a two-thirds majority for most of the period since 2010, allowing it to adopt a new constitution in 2011.

Orbán describes his system as an "illiberal democracy". The EU has criticised Hungary over the rule of law, media freedom and corruption, freezing some funds. Hungary has opposed EU policies on migration and maintained relations with Russia. The April 2026 parliamentary election was the most competitive in years, with the new opposition Tisza party, led by Péter Magyar, mounting a strong challenge to Fidesz.

economy.heading: An export-oriented economy
paragraphs: Hungary has an export-oriented, industrial economy. Car manufacturing by German companies such as Audi, Mercedes-Benz and BMW is central, and the country has attracted large Asian investments in electric vehicle batteries. Pharmaceuticals, electronics, food and agriculture are also important.
Hungary uses the forint rather than the euro. It experienced high inflation in 2022–23, among the highest in the EU, and the economy has been heavily dependent on EU funds and Russian energy.
